{{nihongo|'''Okuni Shrine'''|大國神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Kōzuke Province]].

{{commons category|Category:Okuni-jinja (Isesaki)}}
[[ja:大國神社 (伊勢崎市)]]

{{wikidata link|Q17221549|commons|Category:Okuni-jinja (Isesaki)|ja|大國神社 (伊勢崎市)|check_date=2026-05-18}}

== Overview ==
[[File:Okuni-jinja (Isesaki) torii.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Torii]]
'''Ōkuni Shrine''' (大國神社, おおくにじんじゃ; also written 大国神社) is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|ja|神社|lt=Shinto shrine|lt_ja=神社}} at Sakai-Shimofuchina (しもふちな), {{ill|Isesaki, Gunma|ja|伊勢崎市|lt=Isesaki|lt_ja=伊勢崎市}}, {{ill|Gunma Prefecture|ja|群馬県|lt=Gunma Prefecture|lt_ja=群馬県}}. It is a {{ill|Shikinaisha|ja|式内社|lt=Shikinaisha|lt_ja=式内社}} (small), and under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代社格制度|lt=former shrine ranking system|lt_ja=旧社格}} it was a {{ill|Gō-sha|ja|郷社|lt=district shrine|lt_ja=郷社}}. Tradition dates its founding to the ninth year of {{ill|Emperor Suinin|ja|垂仁天皇|lt=Emperor Suinin|lt_ja=垂仁天皇}}, the eleventh emperor; the main sanctuary is a three-bay {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|ja|流造|lt=nagare-zukuri|lt_ja=流造}} building, and the annual festival is held on 22 October.<ref name="chimei"/>

It is also called "Daigo Hime-no-miya" (第五姫宮, "shrine of the fifth princess") and "Gogo-no-miya" (五護之宮).<ref name="chimei"/>

=== Deities ===
'''Principal deity'''
* '''{{ill|Ōkuninushi|ja|大国主|lt=Ōkuninushi no Mikoto|lt_ja=大国主命}}''' (おおくにぬしのみこと)<ref>The deities are as given on the information board in the grounds.</ref>

'''Secondary deities'''
* {{ill|Hibasu-hime|ja|日葉酢媛命|lt=Hibasu-hime no Mikoto|lt_ja=日葉酢媛命}} (ひばすひめのみこと): empress of Emperor Suinin.
* Nuhataniirihime no Mikoto (渟葉田瓊入媛命, ぬはたにいりひめのみこと)
* Matonohime no Mikoto (真砥野媛命, まとのひめのみこと)
* Azaminiirihime no Mikoto (薊瓊入媛命, あざみにいりひめのみこと)
* Takanohime no Mikoto (竹野媛命, たかのひめのみこと)
*: All are daughters of {{ill|Tanba no Michinushi|ja|丹波道主命|lt=Tanba no Michinushi|lt_ja=丹波道主王命}}. They are said to have been brought here from Anō township in Tanba Province and enshrined together in the fifteenth year of Emperor Suinin, and the names "Daigo Hime-no-miya", "Gogo-no-miya" and "Gokō-gū" (五后宮, "shrine of the five empresses") are said to come from these five goddesses.<ref name="board"/>

'''Merged deities'''
* {{ill|Mizuhanome|ja|ミヅハノメ|lt=Mizuhanome|lt_ja=罔象女}}: deity of the former Mitarashi Shrine.
* {{ill|Susanoo|ja|スサノオ|lt=Susanoo no Mikoto|lt_ja=素戔嗚尊}} and {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|lt=Kotoshironushi no Mikoto|lt_ja=事代主命}}: deities of the former Yasaka Shrine.

== History ==
=== Founding ===
According to the shrine's tradition (the ''Ōkuni Gogo-gū Engi'' of the {{ill|Meiwa|ja|明和|lt=Meiwa|lt_ja=明和}} era, 1764–1772) and the ''Isesaki Fudoki'', in the ninth year of Emperor Suinin the people were suffering from unseasonable wind and rain, and the emperor sent {{ill|Kudara no Kurumi|ja|百済車臨|lt=Kudara no Kurumi|lt_ja=百済車臨}} to the eastern provinces.<ref name="chimei"/><ref name="board"/> Arriving here, Kurumi met Ōkuninushi washing his hands at the Mitarashi pond and begged him to quell the nation's troubles.<ref name="board"/> Ōkuninushi then vanished, and a pool (''fuchi'') formed where he had stood, the origin of the place name "Fuchina".<ref name="board"/> The emperor later rewarded Kurumi, had him worship at this shrine and gave him the land.<ref name="board"/> In the ninth month of Suinin 15, the shrine of the five princesses was brought from Anō in Tanba and enshrined here as well.<ref name="board"/>

Another view of the founding rests on the ''Kōzuke no Kuni Jinmyōchō'', which lists both "Ōkunitama Myōjin" and "Kōritama Myōjin" (くにたまみょうじん, no longer extant) under Sai District. It takes ''kunitama'' to be the god of the provincial governor and ''kōritama'' the god of the district governor.<ref name="kamigami"/> This shrine, corresponding to the former, would then have been newly founded when the district governor of the area was given the honorary title "Kamitsukenu no Kuni no Miyatsuko" (see below).<ref name="kamigami"/> On this view, from the records that {{ill|Hinokumabe no Oitoji|ja|檜前部老刀自|lt=Hinokumabe no Oitoji|lt_ja=檜前部老刀自}} (ひのくまべのおいとじ, also Hinokuma no Kimi Oitoji)<ref group="original">''Shoku Nihongi'', Tenpyō Jingo 2 (766), twelfth month, twelfth day.</ref> was granted the name "Kamitsukenu no Sai no Asomi" (かみつけのさいのあそん)<ref group="original">''Shoku Nihongi'', Jingo Keiun 1 (767), third month, sixth day.</ref> and later the title "kuni no miyatsuko of the home province" (Kamitsukenu no Kuni no Miyatsuko),<ref group="original">''Shoku Nihongi'', Jingo Keiun 2 (768), sixth month, sixth day.</ref> it is inferred that the Hinokumabe family were the district governors of Sai.<ref name="kamigami"/> A connection has also been suggested with the Jūsanpōzuka site (じゅうさんぽうづかいせき) north-west of the shrine, which is thought to be the site of the Sai district office.<ref name="kamigami"/>

"Fuchina township, Sai District", which appears in the ''{{ill|Wamyō Ruijushō|ja|和名類聚抄|lt=Wamyōshō|lt_ja=和名抄}}'', is identified with this area.<ref>''Gunma-ken no Chimei'', entry "Shimofuchina site".</ref>

=== Outline ===
The shrine is not mentioned in the national histories.<ref name="kamigami"/> According to its tradition, in {{ill|Jingo-keiun|ja|神護景雲|lt=Jingo Keiun|lt_ja=神護景雲}} 1 (767) the ''uneme'' of Sai repaired the shrine buildings on imperial command.<ref name="board"/>

The ''{{ill|Engishiki Jinmyōchō|ja|延喜式神名帳|lt=Engishiki Jinmyōchō|lt_ja=延喜式神名帳}}'' lists it as "Ōkuni Shrine, {{ill|Sai District, Gunma|ja|佐位郡|lt=Sai District|lt_ja=佐位郡}}, Kōzuke Province", a {{ill|Shikinaisha|ja|式内社|lt=Shikinaisha|lt_ja=式内社}}. Sai District was the forerunner of {{ill|Sawa District, Gunma|ja|佐波郡|lt=Sawa District|lt_ja=佐波郡}}, formed in the Meiji period by merging Sai and {{ill|Nawa District, Gunma|ja|那波郡|lt=Nawa District|lt_ja=那波郡}}.

In the ''Kōzuke no Kuni Jinmyōchō'', the Ichinomiya text lists "Ōkuni Daimyōjin, Senior First Rank" twelfth of the twelve guardian shrines, and the ''Gunsho Ruijū'' text likewise lists "Ōkunitama Daimyōjin, Senior First Rank" twelfth of twelve; the Sōja text has no such entry among its ten guardian shrines.<ref name="kamigami"/> All three texts list "Ōkunitama Myōjin, Senior First Rank" under Sai District.<ref name="kamigami"/> Whether the guardian-shrine entry and the Sai District entry are the same shrine is disputed, and one view takes the latter to be this shrine and the ''Engishiki'' shrine to be another.<ref name="chimei"/>

In {{ill|Meiji era|ja|明治|lt=Meiji|lt_ja=明治}} 7 (1874) it was made a {{ill|Gō-sha|ja|郷社|lt=district shrine|lt_ja=郷社}} under the {{ill|Modern system of ranked Shinto shrines|ja|近代社格制度|lt=modern shrine ranking system|lt_ja=近代社格制度}}.<ref name="board"/> In Meiji 42 (1909) it was designated a shrine eligible for offerings of food and cloth (''shinsen heihaku-ryō'').<ref name="board"/>

=== Divine rank ===
* Senior First Rank (guardian-shrine entry of the ''Kōzuke no Kuni Jinmyōchō''): written "Ōkuni Daimyōjin" (Ichinomiya text) and "Ōkunitama Daimyōjin" (''Gunsho Ruijū'' text); not in the Sōja text.<ref name="kamigami">''Nihon no Kamigami'', entry "Ōkuni Jinja".</ref>
*: <small>Note: all three texts list "Ōkunitama Myōjin, Senior First Rank" under Sai District, but whether it is the same as the guardian-shrine entry is disputed.<ref name="chimei">''Gunma-ken no Chimei'', entry "Ōkuni Jinja".</ref></small>

== Grounds ==
[[File:Okuni-jinja (Isesaki) haiden-1.JPG|thumb|200px|right|Shrine buildings]]
The {{ill|Honden|ja|本殿|lt=honden|lt_ja=本殿}} is a three-bay {{ill|Nagare-zukuri|ja|流造|lt=nagare-zukuri|lt_ja=流造}} building with a ''chidori-hafu'' gable and a ''noki-karahafu'' over the eaves, roofed with copper sheet.<ref name="board"/> It is said to have been built in {{ill|Kansei|ja|寛政|lt=Kansei|lt_ja=寛政}} 5 (1793), in the {{ill|Edo period|ja|江戸時代|lt=Edo period|lt_ja=江戸時代}}.<ref name="board"/> The ''heiden'' was built in {{ill|Shōwa era|ja|昭和|lt=Shōwa|lt_ja=昭和}} 5 (1930). The ''haiden'' is five bays wide and three and a half deep, built in {{ill|Bunka (era)|ja|文化 (元号)|lt=Bunka|lt_ja=文化}} 1 (1804).<ref name="board"/>

The grounds also hold a ''sekidō'' (石幢, a kind of Buddhist stone tower), also called the "stone lantern of Mitarashi".<ref name="board"/> It bears an inscription of {{ill|Entoku|ja|延徳|lt=Entoku|lt_ja=延徳}} 2 (1490), in the {{ill|Muromachi period|ja|室町時代|lt=Muromachi period|lt_ja=室町時代}},<ref name="sekido"/> and is said to have been dug up beside the nearby Mitarashi pond.<ref name="board">Information board in the shrine grounds.</ref> It stands 2.38 metres high in all, built up on a square stone base from shaft, middle seat, light chamber, roof and finial.<ref name="board"/> It shows the style of the Muromachi period<ref name="board"/> and is designated an important cultural property of the city.

North-east of the shrine is the site of the Mitarashi pond where Ōkuninushi is said to have washed his hands.<ref name="chimei"/> The Mitarashi Shrine stood there until it was merged into this shrine in Meiji 40 (1907).<ref name="chimei"/>

=== Subsidiary shrines ===
* Sengen Shrine
::[Deity] {{ill|Konohanasakuya-hime|ja|コノハナノサクヤビメ|lt=Konohanasakuya-hime no Mikoto|lt_ja=木華開耶姫命}}<ref name="sengen">Notice board on the history of the Sengen Shrine (set up February 1990).</ref>
::After the government order merging shrines into one per village was lifted after the Pacific War, Konohanasakuya-hime was enshrined in the empty building of the former Mitarashi Shrine at Mitarashi pond, which came to be called the Sengen Shrine. At some point that building was moved to Ōkuni Shrine and merged with it.<ref name="sengen"/>
* Fuchina Tenmangū
::[Deity] {{ill|Sugawara no Michizane|ja|菅原道真|lt=Sugawara no Michizane|lt_ja=菅原道真}}<ref name="tenmangu">Notice board on the history of the Tenmangū.</ref>
::A building was put up in July 1982 (Shōwa 55) and the Fuchina Tenmangū was moved into it.<ref name="tenmangu"/>
* Mitarashi Shrine
::[Deity] {{ill|Mizuhanome|ja|ミヅハノメ|lt=Mizuhanome|lt_ja=罔象女}}<ref name="engi">Notice board ''Kōzuke no Kuni Shikinai Jūnisha Ōkuni Jinja Engi'' (set up October 1997).</ref>
::The Mitarashi Shrine that stood at Mitarase-numa in Hachiki-chō, Isesaki, was merged here on 25 March 1907 (Meiji 40).<ref name="heisei">''Heisei Matsuri Data'' (Association of Shinto Shrines, June 1995).</ref>
* Yasaka Shrine
::[Deity] {{ill|Kotoshironushi|ja|事代主神|lt=Kotoshironushi no Mikoto|lt_ja=事代主命}}<ref name="engi"/>
::Merged 25 March 1907 (Meiji 40).<ref name="heisei"/>
* Gozu Tennō Shrine: merged in Tenna 1 (1681)
* Fujitake Shrine: merged February 1918 (Taishō 7)
* Nishinomiya Shrine, Suwa Shrine<ref>The subsidiary shrines are as given on the information board in the grounds.</ref>
* Hachiman Shrine, Inari Shrine, Sukunahikona Shrine
* Jishin Shrine, Hōsō Shrine, Sumiyoshi Shrine
* Taga Shrine, Marishiten-gū
* Sarutahiko Ōkami, Mitsuhanome-gami
* Konjin, and eighteen others

== Festivals ==
* Spring festival (3 April)<ref>The festivals are as given on the information board in the grounds.</ref>: minor festival.
* Summer festival (day of the Sakai-machi Fureai Festival): middle festival.
* Autumn festival (last Sunday of October): great festival, at which the "Shimofuchina lion dance" is performed.

The lion dance at the autumn festival had died out but was revived in the 1950s–60s.<ref name="shishimai"/> Its school is said to be the Hibasami school.<ref name="board"/> An inscription on its prop box suggests it was established by {{ill|Shōtoku (era)|ja|正徳 (日本)|lt=Shōtoku|lt_ja=正徳}} 1 (1711), and its origin is thought to be earlier.<ref name="board"/> As the "Shimofuchina lion dance" it is designated an intangible folk cultural property of the city.<ref name="shishimai"/>

== Cultural properties ==
=== Isesaki City designated ===
* Important cultural property
** Sekidō of Ōkuni Shrine: designated 10 February 1967.<ref name="sekido">[http://www.city.isesaki.lg.jp/www/contents/1354673497110/index.html Sekidō of Ōkuni Shrine] (Isesaki City website).</ref>
* Important intangible folk cultural property
** Shimofuchina lion dance: designated 15 June 2006.<ref name="shishimai">[http://www.city.isesaki.lg.jp/www/contents/1355811532601/index.html Shimofuchina lion dance] (Isesaki City website).</ref>
